en: From a manuscript in the Oriental Institute Library, Baroda, Accession No. 13118, beginning on folio 12v, line 5: "Now, as for Khecarī—Khecarī is the final mudrā; she goes to the Brahma-randhra without delay."
Suṣumnā is known as Mūrcchā, and Laṃvikā is known as Vācakā.
Without the sequence there is no scripture, and without the scripture there is no sequence.
Having understood the scripture endowed with the sequence, one becomes illustrious on this earth.
The wise physician should fashion an instrument resembling the tongue in shape and small enough to cut it; he should also make a small blade resembling the leaf of the *snuhī* plant.
Having observed the knot at the base of the tongue, he should excise it to the size of a sesame seed.
Having powdered two niṣkas, one niṣka, and half a niṣka of harītakī, dry ginger,
and rock salt, one should rub [the mercury] with that powder according to the previously described method for the shaking of the śakti.

One should practice again; when the seventh day arrives, one should cut [the hair] to the size of a sesame seed by means of the sequence of cutting and so forth, until it reaches the middle of the eyebrows. 6.
For that long, one should gradually perform the recitation of Śrīnivāsa;
herein lies this tradition of Haṭhayoga:
[the syllables] *śi*, *śu*, *laṃ*, *vi*, *kā*, *vā*, *ga*, *na*, *ā*, *tī*, *taṃ*, *na*, *ga* emerge from within the tip of the index finger.
When the earth falls during the conjunction of the *laṃvikā*, the binding of the tongue occurs in that which falls; for the tongue exists by way of being a reflection of the *laṃvikā*.
Furthermore, because it is a subtle form of a knot (*granthi*), it is still visible today to all men through direct perception.
In that very place, it appears that the breaking of the subtle knot which acts as the binder for attaining the *laṃvikā* must be performed.

In the chapter proclaimed by the Supreme Lord, however, one should cut off with a weapon resembling the leaf of the *snuhī* plant— extremely sharp, smooth, and stainless— a portion of the tongue equal in length to a single hair (*romamātra*). 1.
"Indeed, by cutting away even a single hair's breadth [of the veil], the heart of the authors has been extracted by Bilavana; this has been stated by me. 2.
But Dattātreya says:
When the tongue enters the hollow of the skull and moves in reverse,
and the gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, that becomes the Khecarī Mudrā.
There is neither disease nor death, nor sleep, hunger, or thirst.
He who knows the Khecarī Mudrā shall not suffer fainting;
he is not afflicted by disease, nor is he tormented by karma, nor is he oppressed by illness or even by death, through this very Mudrā. 4–5.
The authors of the Haṭhapradīpikā, however, state:

"By means of cutting, moving, and milking, one should increase [the tongue] through the sequence of the digits (kalā) until it reaches the space between the eyebrows; at that time, the siddhi of Khecarī is attained. (1)
Since there is no mention of the specific methods for cutting [the channels], that approach is characterized by forcefulness;
therefore, this doctrine—which is difficult for those of dull intellect to understand—should be accepted.
Now, I shall describe the conventions according to the path shown by the Guru.
In the absence of the chain of conventional symbols, how could there be the Khecarī?

It has the form of a serpent, complete with its coils, measuring two chains in length, including the head-ornament (kharpara), and characterized by the convention of six spans (vitasti) in total length. 4.

The wise know it as an excellent, very long instrument made of two chains, twenty finger-breadths in length, provided with rings and a skull-cup like a snake, which effects the production of the *laṃbikā*.

One should insert the tongue into the cavity of the palate with a chain; when it reaches the path of the Suṣumṇā, Khecarī is accomplished. Once the sealing by Khecarī has occurred, the embodied soul does not abandon the body.
Having abandoned the body at the end of the kalpa, he goes to the abode of Brahmā. When the vital breath has entered the suṣumnā, the sound is heard in eight ways,
like a bell, a drum, a conch, the ocean, a lute, a flute, fire, and a net.
Just as [the wind] blows through the fibers of a lotus stalk,
so too, in the body of a yogi who has been bitten by the serpent of the Lord of Death (Yama), or by Kāśyapa and other nāgas, or even by Takṣaka, the poison is unable to take effect.
The yogi who drinks the stainless nectar of the stream, which possesses the beauty of surging waves, remains free from defects; with a body as tender as a lotus stalk, he lives for a long time.
If the tongue, which constantly secretes saliva, were to lick the tip of the *laṃvikā* [the uvula],
it would taste like salt, pungent, bitter, or milk, and likewise like wine or clarified butter.
It is held that [the breath] reaches the opening at the tip of the tongue through all the channels without exception,

by means of which path one may proceed to the lunar digit (*cāndrī kalā*). Through this, the accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as the power of speaking like a maiden (*kanyāvāda*), the power of speaking like a ram (*vilāvāda*), and the power of speaking with flavor (*rasavāda*) are attained.
The yoginīs proceed from them;
they are Vajrā, Likhī, Carī, Trikuṇṭhā, Rvā, Hiṭhā, Golīṭhā, Śikharā, Triṃśaṅkhī, Vajrā, Oṃkārī, and Ūrddhanālā, located in the eyebrows, the face, and the mouth. 12–13.
Piṅgalā, Dāminī, Sūryā, Yamī, Nākākṣarā, as well as Kālāgnirudrī and Caṇḍī— these are the ones named Piṅgalā.
Furthermore, Iḍā, Candrāsinī, Vālī, Gaṅgā, and Vāmā are known as the left [channels].
The words denoting *iḍā* have been proclaimed as synonyms.
The tongue is expressed by the word "cow" (*go*), for it enters the palate;
that indeed is the eating of cow's flesh, which destroys even the greatest sins. 15–16.
"One should constantly eat beef and drink the nectar of the gods (amaravāruṇī)," thus says the second instruction in the *Haṭharatnāvalī*.
